utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager. May I thank you Your Honour for the extra time you gave me this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, it has to be emphasised, first of all, that due to the continuing illness of Judge Fassi Fihri, today we proceed under Rule 15 bis. As planned, let me please start making reference to the Status Conference yesterday. As consented and explicitly consented by the parties, we prepared yesterday the admission into evidence of some documents. Yesterday, Judge Vassylenko took the opportunity to go through all the documents. Later on, we discussed these, and we came to the following conclusion: That based on this, the documents contained in List 7 all can be admitted into evidence explicitly, also Number 299 where, during the Status Conference, it was not yet quite sure whether or not this document was ripe for admission. But in the meantime, the Office of the Prosecutor provided us with the complete English translation of this document. Therefore, there is no reason not to introduce and admit this into evidence. On the other hand, I have to recall that a document with the ERN number 03048407 is only - and this is true also for the future - is only provisionally admitted as Exhibit S318 because the Defence asked for the best possible original and to decide on the basis of this then available document. So therefore, to conclude, it is hereby confirmed that all the documents in List 7 are admitted into evidence under the numbers given to those documents provisionally yesterday. In addition, the following documents that had been earlier already a discussion were admitted: S254, S267, S73. I have to recall that for the following documents, there are still some problems: S242, S217, S210, S227B, S157-1. Thank you. I just now got the hint not as the transcript reads, and apparently I gave the wrong number. It's not S318, but 308, which was not admitted into evidence from List 7. We were aware of the objections given by the Defence, but based on the discussion yesterday, we came to these conclusions. And for this purpose, please, the transcript of yesterday be part of today's transcript following immediately the pagination of today's transcript. All the reasons and the discussions then can be immediately found on the basis of this entire transcript. Finally, I have to add that to Witness 65 ter Number 16, pseudonym A, is attached and the additional documents provided by the OTP are admitted under Rule 92 bis save the diary, diary which was not translated, but the parties agree that it's not necessary to have these parts translated. The necessary parts form part of the witness's testimony as such. May I ask the parties, do you consent to this procedure? OTP, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, subject to the same agreement the Defence made yesterday, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We also consent to these proceedings, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we then come to today's witness and first of all hear what about protective measures? Normally it changes on a last-minute basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'm afraid because of yesterday's slightly dramatic proceedings and events in Brdjanin/Talic, I never saw him and asked him if he was content. As far as I know, he will testify in open session and no pseudonym required. And I think he would have mentioned it. But perhaps it might be just as well if before his name is given in open court, we just ask whether he is content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told by - helpfully by Ms. Karper as ever - that we have here the original of S308. If anybody wants to see that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, can we do it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And S318 as well, so it's 308 and 318 are both here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, can I just mention something else, normal circumstances, you would have had, and Mr. Lukic, an extra document from me, simply detailing two matters that the witness spoke to me about yesterday. I've told Mr. Lukic that there was a problem yesterday, as I say, and I didn't have an opportunity to put this into writing, but he doesn't object. Firstly, the witness told me that although he knew Dr. Stakic, or knew of him, because he was another doctor, he had never met him and wasn't aware that he was anything to do with politics. And secondly, he told me of an incident that took place in Trnopolje where a woman was shot, but it seems that Mr. Lukic was aware of this already. So I'm passing this on in advance. I'm sorry that it wasn't in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. There shouldn't be an obstacle --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- Such extreme health problems with another accused in another case, no doubt, this has priority. I don't see any obstacle to start immediately with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the usher please escort the witness into the courtroom. Could we please, to be on the safe side, start in private session and ask the witness whether or not there is due cause shown for any protective measure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'm sorry, it is something I should have asked. I don't believe there will be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, is your name Idriz Merdzanic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, my name is Idriz Merdzanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 2 second of January, 1959, and so you are now aged, by my addition, 43?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you a Bosniak by ethnicity or nationality?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, I want to ask you about the events of 1992, between April and September in particular. But can I just ask you a little bit about your background, first. I think it's right that after leaving school, you attended the faculty of medicine in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you do so between 1978 and 1986?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I attended the medical school, the medical faculty, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think on completing that part of your education, you did your military service with the JNA, in fact, with a helicopter unit?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It is common knowledge that in our country, all military-aged men are liable to mandatory military service, which is what I did. And I was a member of the helicopter unit, but as a physician.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after you had completed your military service, did you get a job in an outpatient clinic as a general practitioner in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes, at the Prijedor health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that was an internship, and thereafter, having passed your final exams and obtained your license to practice, did you get a full-time job as a physician in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The internship lasted one year. It was not specialisation. It was an obligatory internship that one is supposed to do after completing the faculty of medicine. After that, one has to pass the professional examination, which I did, and after that, I was given a permanent post at the Prijedor health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think the Prijedor health centre actually covered a number of different areas including Trnopolje, Kozarac, Omarska, Ljubija, and others.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It covered the entire area of the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in 1991, did you begin working at a clinic which was part of the sawmill in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was first in charge of the local clinic, outpatient clinic, in Trnopolje. And in addition to that, I was also assigned to the sawmill outpatient clinic in Trnopolje, but that was only, as far as I remember, twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm sorry. Did you say Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct. I was in charge of the Trnopolje outpatient clinic, and I worked as a physician in Trnopolje. And in addition to that outpatient clinic, I was given an assignment at the sawmill in Kozarac where I was in charge of treating employees of that company.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can I move straight away to the accused in this case, Dr. Milomir Stakic. Did you personally ever meet Dr. Stakic before 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We do not know each other personally, though there is a possibility that we may have passed each other somewhere in the street. But as I said, we don't know each other personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you yourself take any interest in politics after -- between 1990 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was never involved in politics. I didn't have time for that, but I also never expressed any interest in politics, and I am not interested in politics to this date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of Dr. Stakic's entry into political life?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the fact that he was involved in politics, but I heard that he was working in Omarska as a physician there, that he got a job there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I, then, move to asking you, please, a little bit, just about events before April of 1992. We know that the village of Kozarac, for example, was primarily a Muslim village. You, yourself, I think were living in Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was living in Prijedor. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the multiparty elections in 1990, were there any problems or difficulties between the various ethnicities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't notice any such thing and did not personally experience any problems. I had many friends amongst Serbs. I think that I had more Serb friends than any other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When the war in Croatia started in the middle of 1991, as far as you were concerned, did that make any difference to relationships between ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think that it did bring about certain change, that is, the JNA had mobilised all military-aged men to fight in Croatia, in the war in Croatia. Muslims and Croats, the majority of them, did not want to respond to this mobilisation whereas all Serbs went and even volunteered in many cases to go to Croatia to fight the war there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did that have any difference on the attitude that Serbs took towards the Muslim or Croatian population in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did make a difference. Even such people who failed to respond to the callup were -- were tracked down by the military police, and then forcibly taken to the front. The result was that both Muslims and Croats had to go into hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move from there to 1992. Did you become aware or hear about any arms being distributed, weapons?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As the war in Croatia had been going on for some time, it was quite natural for people to talk about war, about the events throughout ex-Yugoslavia. It was through these conversations that I found out that most Serbs had been given weapons. Some people said that those weapons had been distributed by the Serbian army, and only given to certain families. On the other hand, most of the Serbs who went to fight in Croatia, once they returned home, they would not bring their weapons back to the army barracks but brought the weapons home instead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when did you first become aware that there were problems arising in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: What problems exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, problems of movement.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as movement is concerned, there was a military unit that had fought in Croatia. It was a combat military unit which took Prijedor overnight literally. They stormed all the important buildings, the municipal building, the courts. They set up checkpoints. And the next morning, on my way to work, I was stopped at a checkpoint. I had to leave my car. I had to open the trunk of my car. I had to produce my documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that was on your way to work where?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to be on my way to work, my work in Trnopolje. But I realised that there would be a lot of difficulty entailed in that, so I went to the health centre in Prijedor in order to ask and find out what was going on and whether it was possible to go to work outside of Prijedor in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was then that I noticed that there were military in the health centre, and they also IDed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to go to work that day in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't think I was able to go to work on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you remember how long before the attack on Kozarac did that incident take place?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So these checkpoints were set up, and the buildings in Prijedor had been taken over. Did you continue -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you continue over the next few weeks your work in Trnopolje and in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The next day, I went to work. I was being stopped and IDed at checkpoints. But apart from that, there was no further difficulty entailed in getting there. There was also a checkpoint at the crossroads outside Kozarac, and there was a tank there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can I move, then, to how things built up. You told us that there was a checkpoint at the crossroads outside Kozarac and a tank. Did you become aware of other army personnel or vehicles in the vicinity of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I did not myself see any, but I heard that both artillery and tanks had arrived in Prijedor and had been deployed at certain strategically important points.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was one of those points around Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. But I do not really know myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how easy after the arrival of artillery and tanks was it for people to leave Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, yes, you could leave Kozarac through the checkpoints. You had checkpoints not only near Kozarac but also in Orlovci, that's between Kozarac and Prijedor. And the other road, if you took the road from Trnopolje for Prijedor, there were also checkpoints along that road. But ever since the ultimatum by the Serbs concerning Kozarac expired, from that moment on, Muslims were no longer allowed to leave Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you about the ultimatum, please. What was the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, what the whole situation was really about is that the ethnic makeup in Kozarac was almost 98 per cent Muslim. And it was the same with the Kozarac police force. The police were supposed to accept Serb insignia and put up Serbian flags all over Kozarac, but they refused to do so. Negotiations took place, and as far as I know Stojan Zupljanin led the Serb party in these negotiations. I can't remember exactly who attended for the Muslim side. I think Esad Sadikovic was there, and some other people from Kozarac and Prijedor, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So there were negotiations. How did the negotiations end up, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think that they were not successful. What I heard is that Stojan Zupljanin did not really come there to negotiate. He gave an ultimatum and gave a deadline. And he said unless his conditions, his requests were met, by that time the army would take Kozarac by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who did you hear about all this from? Did you hear about this from people involved in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I heard about this from my patients and from the personnel, people who worked with me. This was a much debated topic in those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear over the radio or on television any ultimatum about a deadline for the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have a radio?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, we did not have a radio set at the outpatient clinic, but I can't remember anyone telling me about seeing or hearing anything on TV or the local radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were people who were in need of hospital treatment allowed to pass through the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: When the ultimatum expired, people were no longer allowed to leave Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to come on, then, now, please, to any actions that you took before the attack. Did you speak to any Muslim leaders in Kozarac before the attack?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Immediately before the attack, when the ultimatum expired, I heard from people I talked to in Kozarac that Sead Cirkin, who was an active military officer, was trying to organise some sort of defence for Kozarac. I heard that there were some armed people. One of the workers from the sawmill - I can't remember his name now - took me to see Sead Cirkin. I asked him to. I wanted to talk to Sead Cirkin to see what the role of the outpatient clinic would be in the case of an attack. He was staying at the outskirts of Kozarac, not in Kozarac itself. And his answer was not really very specific. He just gave me general guidelines. He told me to stay put at the outpatient clinic and just continue doing my job, and that he and his people in their turn would try to do theirs. Our contact was not very comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as far as that was concerned, namely, that you should continue doing your job at the outpatient clinic, did you obtain any extra supplies?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, we had no extra supplies. Kozarac was cut off, and there was no one to obtain extra supplies from. The only thing we had was a pharmacy in Kozarac itself, so we took the supplies from that pharmacy and brought all the supplies from the pharmacy to the outpatient clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you anticipating that there would be an attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, we didn't think there would be an attack. But later on, you could see from the first floor of the outpatient clinic in the direction of Prijedor, Prijedor and Hambarine, and from the direction of Ljubija, you could see explosions clearly at night. You could see houses burning. Then we heard stories from people that Carakovo and Hambarine had been under artillery fire for two or three days, and that everything had already been burned down. I think some people may have been able to get in touch with other people through radio communication. At any rate, the phone lines were down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I want to come now, please, to the actual attack itself. Can you remember the date that the attack started at this stage?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The attack started on the 24th of May, I think in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When it started --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' correction: Around noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When it started, were you actually in the clinic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you, please, now to have a look at some photographs of the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are new exhibits, I think, which were handed in to Your Honours and to the Defence yesterday. No, I'm told you don't have these. Can I ask they be handed in now. I think the copies were being made yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, is this once again a collection of several photographs and additional photographs that we attach only one number, and then continue -1, -2 as usual?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland and Ms. Karper are very keen that they should stay under S15 and be added on to those. They think it easier if you keep the photographs together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Shouldn't be a problem. If we may hear what would be the next available dash under S15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are four photographs numbered respectively 0039-3194, 5, 6, and 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They are taken, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From this follows, the photo ending with 94 will be S15-37; 95, -38; 96, -39; 98, -40. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, the date they were taken can be seen, It was in February -- it's American date, so it's written backwards, but it's the 20th of February, 1996. Yes, I wonder if they could be shown to the doctor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look at please, first of all, the one that's marked 3198. I've forgotten what number that is now. But it's the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You'll see it coming up on the screen, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if we can make it clearer. It's an awful picture on the screen. Any way of zooming in on it or making it clearer? No. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise that as a photograph of the Kozarac clinic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the Kozarac clinic. This is the entrance. On the left-hand side, there's a path. There used to be a gate here. On this side and to the right, you can see the entrance to the outpatient clinic. That's the south side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if you could be handed a pointer, and if you just indicate on -- you'll see the photographs next to you here. It is going to be turned around. Just indicate again. The entrance to the clinic was where?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The entrance itself here. There's a few steps here. And then here we had a gate. There was a yard outside and a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. At the time in 1992, was there -- were there any markings on it to indicate that this was a clinic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were no very conspicuous internal signs, but on the roof there may have been a very huge red or white cross, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Kozarac itself, where was the sawmill when looking at the main road of Kozarac, how far back?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The sawmill was just off the main road at the junction. On the way into Kozarac from the junction, the sawmill was the first building on the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we can just establish this, could you be shown the map which is Exhibit S146.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, we'll have it put on the ELMO. We'll take the photograph away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just using the same pointer, indicate to us on that where the...

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the junction here, that's where the sawmill was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes, thank you. And then can we look at the other photographs, please, next, if we go to the one that had 3194, which is S15-37. Is that a close-up of the entrance?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the entrance to the clinic. And on the left-hand side next to the steps, you can see the entrance to the cellar. That's where we had to go when the shelling began.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The damage that we can see -- now, these photographs were taken some -- just under four years later. But was that damage there when you left Kozarac after the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, probably some of the damage changed with time. But the windows were shattered and the walls had suffered heavy damage. And outside the entrance was where shells kept falling. But most shells were falling from the north, from Mount Kozara, and from the left. The shells were falling from the direction to the left of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If you look then just at the remaining --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The image we were looking at before, you could see that all the windows were shattered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going to look at another photograph which is 3195, which is S15-38.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Here you can see the walls pimpled by bullets or shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, if you wouldn't mind, turn towards the photograph itself and indicate it. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, right. All these marks here, shrapnel marks, not a single window. Look at the roof here, you can see that the roof, too, was burned through in several places. It's a bit difficult to notice, but even here outside in the yard, there are craters created by shells falling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The signs that are visible on the wall in the circles, were those on the wall of the clinic before the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness please be asked to repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the answer, I'm sorry Doctor. The interpreters didn't catch that.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. This came about during the shelling. And prior to the shelling, the building was in good condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. We can see on the walls there's a sort of circle with a cross of sorts on them. Were those there before the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. I can't remember ever seeing those there prior to the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do they have any significance that you know of? What do they mean?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, if we look, please, at 3196, which has got the number now S15-39, I think we can more clearly see the damage, the markings, that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Only from the north side, you must know, the damage was greater than to the south side of the building. The side of the building facing south.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what we're looking at, south-facing side of the building?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the south side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. Now, you told us, before we looked at the photographs, that the shelling, the attack, started around noon on the 24th of May. At the time you were in the clinic, were there other medical personnel there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You're quite right; I was not alone at the clinic. There were other medical personnel there together with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you name the people who were there with you, please.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Mensur Kusuran, also a physician was there, too. Azra was there. She is a veterinarian, and her husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before we go on, can you tell us, what was Azra's surname?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. She was a veterinarian. And her husband. Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. She was a veterinarian, and she also worked in Kozarac as a vet. There was a midwife there. We all called her Babica, midwife, because she used to work as a midwife but was now working as a nurse in Kozarac. Her husband was also there. His name was Mujo, who was a paramedic. Then there was Vasif Gutic, a medical student. A woman by the name of Goga who lived in the neighbourhood. She was a Serb, and she had come to the clinic to help us. Then there was a young woman there by the name of Lejla. A couple whose last name was Husidic. The woman's name was Albina, and his name was Senad. And there was also Dr. Pasic who had come to the clinic after the start of the shelling. His house was right next to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, how did you first become aware of the attack?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time the shells started to fall around.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the shelling was going to start that day? In other words, had there been any prior warning as far as you were concerned the town was to be shelled that day?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. At least, I was not aware of that. We, at the clinic, didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So the shelling started. Were you able to tell, because of your military service, where the shells came from? In other words, were they artillery, tanks?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were several of us at the clinic. Naturally, we discussed it. We tried to figure out what would be the best room for us and for the wounded, where we should accommodate the wounded. And we discussed the layout of the hospital, where was the most dangerous side of the hospital. And we concluded that the most sensitive area was the one exposed to Kozara mountain. The majority of the shells were coming from that direction and that is why we decided to go to the cellar which was located at the south side of the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How long did that shelling go on for?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The shelling lasted for about two days with brief lulls. The next day, around noon, there was a lull in the shelling, but on the whole it lasted for about two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any what could be considered military targets near where your clinic was, in other words machine-gun posts or artillery returning fire?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. There was nothing of that kind in the vicinity of Kozarac, and I don't think there was anything of any military interest in Kozarac. There were only civilians in Kozarac, except for the Cirkin group of men who were outside Kozarac actually. But I didn't notice, as far as the Muslim side is concerned, any checkpoints or any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was anybody given an opportunity to leave Kozarac before the shelling began? In other words, women or children or the elderly?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, initially, that is, prior to the attack, I was thinking about leaving Kozarac and going home. But then people started coming in, people who had been turned back at the Orlovci checkpoint. The Serbs manning the checkpoint there IDed people, and those who were from Kozarac were returned. I know that because there were two pregnant women just about to give birth who were sent back to Kozarac. And I delivered their babies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that normal? Would the clinic normally deal with the delivery of babies?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, we never delivered babies in Kozarac. There was a maternity ward in Prijedor, and one in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of that shelling, did you treat people who were injured as a result? Or if not the shelling, any further attacks?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Those who managed to reach us despite the shelling were given assistance to the extent we were able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were those who reached you, were they injured from the shelling, in other words, the debris, or were they injured for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We had a young man at the clinic who claimed that he had been wounded with a shrapnel to his big toe. We had another man who had an entry gunshot wound to his chest. But it must have been fired -- the bullet must have been fired from far away because he was in relatively good shape.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say relatively far away, what made you say that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: If fire is opened from a rifle, and if a person is hit, then the wound is deeper if the bullet was fired from a close distance. In that case, the bullet also exits the body of the person. He was wounded to his chest, to the right area of the chest. And I think that the bullet stopped somewhere in his bones. It did not actually get through his body.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The man who - the boy - I'm sorry, the young man who had a toe injured, what did you do in relation to him as far as treatment was concerned?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, the toe was practically ripped off. There was very tissue left, and we had to severe it. We cleaned his wound and applied bandages to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to the man who had been shot in the chest? Did he survive?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: From what I heard, he survived. The next day, he went with us to another location. He ended up in Omarska, I think. But whether he survived Omarska, that, I don't know. There was another patient there, a Serb, who had a shrapnel wound to his abdomen, to his stomach. He had been brought to the clinic by Muslims who tried to help him. He was a forest keeper from Kozarac, and he was wearing the usual uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you treat any children who were injured as a result of the attack?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Some children were wounded during the attack, but we admitted them only the next day after the clinic had been relocated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what about women?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We had women, too, wounded women. But also at the other location, on the following day. While we were still there at the clinic, we had another civilian who had been brought in dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say that you went to another location on the following day. How did you achieve that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We noticed and were told by the people who had managed to reach us that it was actually very difficult to get to the clinic. We heard that the majority of the civilian population was afraid, and that most of them had left Kozarac and gone to the woods in panic. And this is why we tried to leave that area ourselves. We went towards the Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where did you establish your second clinic, as it were, second location of a clinic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The second location of the clinic was at the outskirts of Kozarac town on the left side of the main road. It was sheltered by a small wood and a hill. It was housed in a building which was not finished. It was located near a creek. The building itself did not have any doors or windows, but it was naturally protected so that from the direction of Prijedor and from the Kozara mountain, there could be no shells that would eventually hit this building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did you yourself try and speak to the authorities in respect of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the time, we had two children at the clinic who were dying. We were practically unable to help them, and I was very upset by the fact. We had other wounded people, of course, but -- well, at any rate, we were located on the ground floor. On the first floor, there was a police vehicle and several police officers there. They were in contact with the military via radio communication, and I asked whether I could try and negotiate the passage of the wounded. And this is what they enabled me to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The police officers, were they Muslims police officers?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. You were allowed, or you tried to negotiate the passage of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the wounded. Do you know who you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was contacted for that purpose in particular, but the same radio station, the same frequency, was used for that purpose. The same as the one which was used for the purposes of negotiating the surrender of Prijedor and the departure of the population from Kozarac. I think that the contact was -- had been established with the military command that was actually attacking Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you -- the person to whom you spoke, what did you say to him that you wanted to do or wanted to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' correction: The surrender of Kozarac, page 25, line 2.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I introduced myself and told him that we had two children with us. There was a little girl there whose lower legs, both of them were completely shattered. She was dying. And then we had another child...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.20. --- Break taken at 10.48 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And evidently, we can continue immediately, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, I realise this is distressing for you to recall these events. So perhaps we can just deal with this fairly quickly. Were you given permission to take these injured children out of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I couldn't evacuate the children or the other wounded who were there. The reply we received was not very specific. The only thing they told us is: "Let all of you balija" - derogatory for Muslims - "die there. We'll kill you all anyway." So that's what the conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, eventually, on the 26th of May, were the terms of surrender agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The police using the same radio stations agreed on the terms of surrender for Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you become aware of any of the terms of the surrender?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, not in detail. What I did know, however, is that the wounded were to lead the way, to be the first in the convoy, those who had survived, followed by policemen, and then -- who in turn were followed by civilians, and they were supposed to walk down the middle of the road. And that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did the shelling then stop that morning?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's when the shelling stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did you decide to do, you the persons who were in the makeshift clinic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We discussed briefly what to do and decided to go back to the original clinic because we assumed that many of the civilians who were either in their own homes or in the woods surrounding Kozarac did not know about the surrender in the first place and that they would come to the clinic seeking help. So that's why we decided to go back to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you got back to the clinic, did further wounded come for your assistance?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. Even the dead body we had left behind was no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that you were worried that people wouldn't hear about the surrender and therefore might come to the clinic. Did you become aware of people who had not found out about the surrender?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I did later on, when we were in the Trnopolje camp. A woman arrived there, her last name was Sahoric, an elderly woman. She had come to the clinic seeking help. And then later she wanted assistance in burying some bodies. She talked to Vasif Gutic and to me. She said that her husband, herself, and a number of neighbours were in the cellar. And that they were found there by soldiers. First they took them out of the cellar, and then threw them back into the cellar, and then a soldier fired a rifle-launched grenade into the cellar. Everyone was killed in the cellar, and she was the only one who remained alive. We sent her to see Major Kuruzovic, and I don't know what happened later. I know that that woman later left, and that she lived in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go back, then, to the events of the 26th of May, after the surrender. You and your colleagues returned to the original clinic. Later that day, did some Serb soldiers arrive?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Three Serb soldiers arrived. They entered the clinic and captured us. One of them was quite a well-known face. He was from Trnopolje. As soon as I remember the name, I'll tell you. I can't remember now, but I'll tell you as soon as I can. Azra, the vet, knew him personally. The other two were persons no one seemed to know, and their accent was heavily Ekavian, which probably implied that they were not from Bosnia but rather from a different region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were any of them wearing any particular type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The one people knew wore, I think, a camouflage olive-drab uniform. And the other two wore green camouflage uniforms. One of them was wearing a red beret, and they all wore the same armbands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did these three soldiers say anything about what was to happen to you at the clinic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The one bearing the beret, he went up to the first floor. He opened all the doors. He kept yelling, saying that everyone was to be killed. The remaining two, including the one people knew, they called the woman who had the name Goga written on her apron, which showed that she was a Serb. So they called her for an interview. And then the soldier from Trnopolje left the building and returned after a short while. He told us then that there would be a lorry arriving soon on to which we were to load the medicines from the clinic, and that we would then be taken somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did a lorry arrive then, a little later?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: After a while, a green military lorry with JNA insignia arrived, and we loaded on to it all the supplies we had at the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the truck leave, then?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, the truck left. And those three soldiers escorted us in a convoy to the centre of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever see that truck and the medical supplies again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness please be asked to repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you just say that again. The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw the lorry again, nor the medical supplies in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Doctor, it would probably help if you pull your chair a little closer to the microphone. That will help. Thank you. Now, as you were taken to the centre of Kozarac, what was the damage like, that you saw?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: What we saw there, and on the way there, soldiers breaking into houses. It was obvious that most of them were just simply looting, taking things out of the houses. One of them tried to use a car to take things away from a house. Once we arrived in the centre of Kozarac, there were at least two tanks there and a lot of soldiers all over the place. We stopped there in the middle of the road. And there was a tree there, and that's where we waited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In a moment, I'm going to ask you to look at a plan that you drew for us of Kozarac so that you can indicate these places. But did you have occasion to pass the mosque?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I did not pass by the mosque, and I really paid no attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you now look, please, at the plan that you provided to the investigator, of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honours -- you were given copies, I'm told. Your Honours, unless there's an objection, could that be marked S321, we believe, Ms. Karper believes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have a number of sketches. Could you please give us the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I could. It's 0103 -- I'm sorry, yes 01035313. And it's entitled "Kozarac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. This would be -- if there are no objections and I can't see any, S3 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 321. And could we make that -1, Your Honour, because there's a couple more sketches I'm going to be asking the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's already 332, registry, can you help us out?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, it would be S321, Your Honour, -1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, we took the pictures as 15. Okay. Then let's start with -1 for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, if you'd like to have a look, we can put the plan on the ELMO and you can look at it. I think you marked for us the main road, the Banja Luka/Prijedor Road, and then the sawmill to the left, as you look at it, of the road going to Prijedor. And then the pharmacy and where the temporary clinic was that you told us about, which is going, as you say, towards the other end of the road. When you were marched down -- taken to Kozarac -- I'm sorry, taken by the soldiers to the centre of Kozarac, where did you end up? Just indicate on the plan.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Right here, this spot here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just while you're looking there, you've marked what appears to be a religious building of some kind to the right of the main Kozarac street. Can you just tell us what that is that you've marked there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You mean the Serb church here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. That's the Serb church?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's the Serb church in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just out of interest, where was the mosque?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I really have no idea. A bit further to the north, I think. It wasn't downtown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. All right, thank you. Now, you say, as you were taken there - that's all, thank you very much - you saw people looting houses. Do you remember, were those houses damaged by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of houses that had been damaged, but not really completely destroyed. You had marks of shelling, roofs caving in, windows shattered. But most of the houses were in rather good condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the usher, I'm not going to be showing the diagram again at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there other people in the centre when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You mean civilians?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Not that I noticed. That's aside from us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, whilst you were standing near this tree in the centre, were you approached by any members of the military?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Nihad Bahonjic, the ambulance driver in Kozarac, was approached by a soldier. I did not know that soldier. He wanted to see his ID. And once he saw his ID, he told him to follow him, and he took him away from our group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did any of you make any inquiry as to why he was being taken away?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Why he was taken away. When a jeep arrived to take us away, too, and when we got into the jeep, they -- I saw they weren't bringing Bahonjic back. So I asked one of the soldiers with a rank, a military rank, what had happened to Nihad Bahonjic, and they answered that they would take care of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How long after he had been taken from your group did the jeep arrive which took you away?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A short or a long time is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, that depends on what exactly you mean by "short" or "long."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: But certainly not more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, after you'd asked what was happening to Mr. Bahonjic, and you were told that they would take care of him, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We were all compelled, forced, to get on to the jeep. And we drove out of Kozarac towards the junction. I tried to pay attention and see which road we were taking. Apparently, we were heading in the direction of Banja Luka, and you could hear sounds of shots fired there. And apparently, Bahonjic was then killed, and Azra claimed later that she saw him killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How old was Mr. Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: He may have been 35, 36 years old at that time. He had a wife and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just again give us the first name of Mr. Bahonjic.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Nihad Bahonjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So you were driven off, and where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At first, we headed towards Prijedor, and then there was a cafe to the left and a dirt track passing by. So we took a left turn. We pulled over by the dirt track. There were several soldiers standing there. Many of them officers with high ranks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you remain in the jeep, or were you made to get out?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We remained in the jeep briefly. Then we got out. They took out of the jeep Senad Husidic. Meanwhile, a bus arrived from Prijedor with women and children. And then they told the rest of us to get on to the bus. Husidic's wife asked what the fate of Senad would be and whether he would join us. But they told her that he was a Green Beret and that he took part in supplying weapons to the local Muslims and that he would have to stay there. His wife then begged them to let him go and said that he had had nothing to do with any of that. And we told them that he was at the clinic with us. And then the higher-ranking officer of the two decided to allow him to get on to the bus. However, as soon as we got to -- as we arrived in Trnopolje, they came for him the next day, and he was then taken to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to him eventually?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he was later transferred to Manjaca from Omarska. At any rate, he survived, and I think later he lived somewhere in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So did the bus then take you to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That bus, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you were familiar with Trnopolje obviously because you had worked there. When you arrived at Trnopolje, was there already a camp which had been set up?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The moment we arrived, we knew nothing about any camps. We couldn't tell if it was a camp or not. There were a lot of soldiers there, civilians, too, women, children. It was only later that we found out that actually it was a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you arrived, where did the bus unload all its passengers, all of you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can point this out to you on one of the photographs or sketches. If you have a sketch of that, perhaps I could point it out to you because it's difficult to explain verbally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I would ask you to look at a sketch that you provided, again, to the investigator which bears the number 0103531.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the last digit, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 4. 314, sorry. It slightly disappeared on my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be, then, 321-2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Can I start speaking?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think the bus stopped here. This is the Prijedor/Trnopolje Road. There was a small path here, a narrow path. And then we got off the bus and took this path. And there were soldiers lined up all along this path. The women stayed behind, and they were sent to this hall. I was recognised, and they said: "Oh, here's our doctor." And they told me to go to the clinic. And then we all went to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I just want to see -- I think we may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You indicated the clinic. May you please, once again, point on the sketch. Is it named "ambulancija" or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it may help if we look at some of the photographs which have already been exhibited as part of S15. It's 15-9. And that may help. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the path I was talking about. Perhaps you can see it here. That's where the bus stopped. We came right here, the women and children were sent to this big hall. And we were then marched over to the clinic. And that building over there, that's the school building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, at that stage, on your arrival, if you can remember, was there anything to indicate that this was a camp, wire or fencing?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Not in the sense of any special fence being put up for the purpose. There was a fence that had been there before. And I don't think any of us even had the idea of a camp in mind. So we didn't even think about such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. When you arrived there and were getting out of the bus, did you recognise any of the soldiers who were there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The soldiers there, no, I think there was this young man who knew me. He approached me. He knew me from the Prijedor airport. His father worked at the airport, too, in some capacity. I can't remember. So he started flying airplanes. But I can't remember knowing any of the soldiers there. There was Rade Baltic, wearing plainclothes. He recognised me, and he said: "Here's our doctor." But the other soldier -- the other soldier said: "Here's our doctor," but he was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The man who approached you from the Prijedor airport, was that Rade Baltic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. Rade Baltic was wearing plainclothes, civilian clothes, and he was from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were you ever aware, at that first stage, of anybody who was in command?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We didn't know really about the command structure. That was already at some point in the afternoon, we were taken to that clinic, and that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally this, on this first afternoon: The soldiers who were there, were you able to understand from their uniforms who they were, what unit?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to tell really. Probably persons who had been mobilised as early as the war in Croatia. And now that the war broke out here, in this area, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any police uniforms there that you noticed or was it all military?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At least I didn't notice any police uniforms. The only uniforms I saw were military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were placed in the clinic. And did you remain in the clinic until the following day?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We remained until the following day. It grew dark very soon. And as night fell, a very loud horrible shooting began. We just threw ourselves on the floor, and we didn't know what was happening. It was only the next day that we found out they were just shooting bullets into the air for fun.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, at what stage was this area which was effectively Trnopolje, at what stage did it become a camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: After several days, we realised that we would not leave. At the beginning, I thought to myself: "Well, I'm just a civilian. Maybe they will just run a check on me and then release me, allow me to go home." But we remained there. Men were no longer allowed to leave the camp unless someone's name was included in a list to be transferred to a different camp. After a while, they started to organise convoys for women, children, and the elderly to transfer these people out of the Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to come on to the convoys and other aspects of Trnopolje in a moment. Can we just look at the general layout. You've shown us and we looked at the photograph of Trnopolje. At some stage, was some kind of wire erected?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. A wire fence was put up when Keraterm and Omarska camps were disbanded. And then a wire fence was put up to contain prisoners from Keraterm and Omarska. But it was only there for a short while. And when journalists began arriving, they took it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the wire was only put up after the Omarska and Keraterm prisoners were transferred there. Was that before or after the arrival of the journalists or both?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The wire fence had been erected prior to the arrival of journalists, and then taken down afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's my fault. Bad question. The transfer of the Omarska prisoners and Keraterm, did that happen before the arrival of the journalists, then, or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Some of them arrived before the arrival of Penny Marshall. That first group included women and underaged people, and the severely ill, sick people, from Omarska. And then the group from Keraterm arrived, and then there was the visit of the journalists after which, sometime around midnight, a large convoy arrived from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before that, and we know that that was August of 1992, what prevented people from leaving Trnopolje the camp? You said men were no longer allowed to leave unless their name was on a list.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Guards were posted around Trnopolje, all around Trnopolje. There were guard posts, and then there was this fence. One could easily jump over that fence, however. But apart from the checkpoints and the guards, even if only a simple line had been drawn on the ground, nobody would dare cross that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. On the diagram that we've just looked at, I wonder if you could have that back again, which is S321-2, can you indicate to us where there were guard posts?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: On this diagram, I marked with this sign the guard posts. They were here, one of them was here on the south side, and then on the road leading to Kozarac, there was another one here. Across the street from the entrance to the clinic, there was another one. Opposite the school near the petrol station. And then one more -- actually, on two more locations, on either sides of the road on this road leading to Kozarac. As for the other side, one was here on the left side when coming from Prijedor. There was a house here, and then a checkpoint next to this house with sand bags. There was a small terrace on this house with a sniper, and then this house here there was another checkpoint, next to this house which was used by them for rest and recuperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of the transcript, what you're indicating in each case is the circle that you've shown with the markings inside. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct. Here, there is a circle. I could have used any other marking, of course. But each of these circles marks a guard post and a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were other checkpoints located outside the camp, further away. But those -- these are the ones that were right next to the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, and once again for the transcript, where did you identify snipers? Can you mention it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, there was a sniper on the upper floor of this house here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you're indicating to the left-hand side of the diagram you drew in the square box, top left-hand corner. And you've written beside it -- can you just read to us what you've written.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The square marks a house. And then the circle underneath --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but to the right of that, this is simply so we can identify it later on the plan, what have you written? There are some words written.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: "Football pitch."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So that's one sniper post. You indicated another one.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of another one. I don't know whether there was any other elsewhere. There was a machine-gun nest on this checkpoint here, I believe. And then on this one here, and then one other there. Whether there were any other snipers, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to be concrete, from the transcript, one could read that you also mentioned a sniper at the bottom where you can read "ograda prodavnice" somewhere in the middle at the bottom on the road. You discussed -- no, further to the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it correct there was also a sniper point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. I know that we noticed one here, on the upper floor of this house. But whether there was one more here, down here, I couldn't tell you with any certainty. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we just identify the places again where you say there were machine-guns. I think you indicated to the guard post at the crossroads. Is that correct, that we can see? There was a machine-gun there? And that's --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I believe it was here, between these two houses. That is, at the back of the house. And next to this house here, where the sniper was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And the machine-guns, which way were they facing, towards the camp or away from the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Towards the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Thank you, yes, that's all we need on the diagram for the moment. Were you the first busload of people to be taken to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, we were not. When we arrived, we found there already a large group of people, mostly women and children. And we learned that they had been there for two days already, that is, since the beginning of the attack on Kozarac. They were probably rounded up on the outskirts of Kozarac, as the attack proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Over the next few days, did other busloads of people arrive?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: New busloads of people kept arriving all the time. The camp was being filled up to its capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were the families kept together, that is, men, women, and children, or were they separated?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They were separated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where were people put? Where did people live?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as Trnopolje is concerned, most of the people were put in the school building. Most of the men were put in the school building. Whereas women and children were put in the community centre, although at the beginning they were mixed. However, later, they were separated. The procedure took -- had already taken place in the villages that were cleansed. It was there that women, children, and elderly were separated from the military-age men. So mostly they were already separated on arrival to Trnopolje. They didn't arrive together, that is to say. And most of the men had probably already been taken to Omarska and Keraterm anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So were there military-aged men arriving at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were, but not in very large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say that the men were placed in the school. And women and children were put into the community centre. Did those two buildings --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct. But once again, it was possible to find men in the school, together with women, especially if there were already too many people there prior to the arrival of their convoys. Then in those cases, they would allow the men to be put into the school building as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Into the building or the --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In which case, they were together with the men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I think there may be possibly a mistranslation. But you are saying if there were too many there, they would put men into the school building as well. Do you mean women into the school building as well? Because you said that men were in the school building.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Women. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did there ever come a time where those buildings were too small to hold the numbers?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Of course, they eventually became too small. Initially, there was no proper accommodation whatsoever. There were no beds, for example. People slept on the floor wearing the same clothes that they were wearing at the time of their arrival. There was no food either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to come on to food and sanitation in a moment. But when the buildings were full up, what happened to the people who were brought to the camp? Where did they stay?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: When the buildings were filled to capacity where they could no longer hold any more people, then the first convoy for women, children, and the elderly was organised. And the convoy was organised from the Trnopolje railway station in...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we then move to --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In cargo carts, and that is how they managed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move next, please, to the question of food. Did the Serb guards provide food for the inmates?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No food was provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did people get food?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, it was agreed that the local population who had not still moved out could bring food into the camp. So many of the local residents brought their food to the camp. This was obviously not enough, but there was simply no other solution at the time. After a while, the Serb Red Cross arrived, and we managed to reach an agreement with them that a local resident who had a large number of cattle, of cows, should bring milk to the camp for the children. We agreed that money should be collected amongst the detainees, and then with the help of the local Serb Red Cross, bread would be brought locally and then brought to the camp the next day and distributed. I have to tell you that the situation was not always the same at the camp. For a while, after that initial period of time, after the local population had also been cleansed, as they called it, and after the local residents stopped bringing in the food, we agreed that the detainees escorted by the guards would be allowed to go into the fields and forage for food there and that they could bring - I don't know - potatoes, vegetables, from the surrounding fields into the camp. And they also brought some stoves from the local houses into the camp, and the food was -- they prepared food for themselves inside the camp. For a brief period of time, the Serbs allowed for a large cauldron to be placed in the camp where food was prepared. But this was not enough, in view of the very large number of people who were detained in the camp. So shortly after that, the cauldron was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Eventually we know that the International Red Cross arrived at the camp and registered people. But up until that time, was there sufficient food to feed all the people who were being kept there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Not enough. We at the clinic didn't receive any food at all, for example. But sometimes local Serbs came to the clinic for examination as well, people who used to be my patients, and they would bring food for me and other personnel at the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about sanitation?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in the camp, there was still some water there, but it was yellowish and obviously not very clean. So we didn't use it. Several days later, the camp ran out of water completely. People couldn't wash, couldn't change their clothes. And -- but people somehow went on living like that in those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about toilets? Were there any toilet facilities available?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were toilets in the school building. However, they soon became filled up and stopped. We didn't have any toilet at the clinic. But we agreed that -- we organised septic pits to be dug out, septic tanks to be dug out near the school building so that people could use those actually simple holes as toilets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when did you become aware that there was somebody who was in charge of this camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, there was a member of the military there. I don't remember exactly what rank he held.
