I think that it was on the second day of my stay there, on the 27th, because we had arrived on the 26th, a Ukrainian woman came to the clinic, Marica Olenjuk. She used to work as a cleaning lady at the clinic. She brought some food, some boiled eggs for us. And she told us that a lady neighbour of hers had come to see her. She was very frightened. She said that soldiers had taken five women up to -- to the upper floor of her house and that she was able to hear screams and cries of those women. And she thought that the soldiers were raping these women in her house. I went out. I wanted to find someone to talk to. I asked for the person who was in charge. There were two men sitting on a crate next to the entrance to the clinic, in the yard in front of the clinic. And they told me that one of them was in charge. So I told him the story I had just heard. I thought that he was the man in charge of Trnopolje at the time. However, after a while -- I mean, this person went away, and I never saw him again. Slobodan Kuruzovic arrived. He was the man in charge of Trnopolje throughout the existence of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you about him in a moment. But can we just complete this episode in relation to your complaining that some women had been raped. Was anything done about that as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I don't know what happened afterwards, whether anything was done afterwards except I had a minor problem myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to you as a result of your reporting this allegation of rape?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The women were allowed to come to the clinic for examination, but they would always be escorted by a guard since somehow we happened to have a lot of boiled eggs that the people had brought us. And each time one such woman would visit us at the clinic, I would give her one or two of these boiled eggs so that they could take them to their children. And one of the soldiers then made allegations against me to the effect that I was preparing a mass killing of Serb children, and that the secret code of the operation was boiled eggs. He showed up with another soldier, and he said that I should go with them. Apparently they were planning to liquidate me. When I came out, I found Rade Baltic there and another person - I always forget his name, the father of this soldier came to the clinic in Kozarac - and asked me what was going on. And I said that the whole thing was a complete nonsense, and I told him that I was being accused of preparing a mass killing of Serb children. He said that I should go back to the clinic and that he would take care of that. He later paid me a visit and told me that he had taken care of that, and that I would have -- I would no longer have any problems. As for the two soldiers, I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we now look at the question of rapes in Trnopolje. You told us there were a number of women there. Did you become aware apart from this incident of other apparent rapes?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In June in particular, there were quite a few rapes. Most of them happened at night. Mostly the individuals involved were not the guards but others who were not on guard duty, people from the outside. They would visit the sleeping quarters of the women at night. They would flash their torch lights at them, and they would take the women out, those whom they liked. And this is what we could observe from the window of the clinic. Some of the women later came to the clinic to ask for help. I believe that the first women to come to the clinic talked to Gutic. And then he came to see me. After we had had several such cases of women coming to our clinic, I talked to Dr. Dusko Ivic, a Serb physician, who sometimes came to the clinic together with Mico Kobas, who was a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you tell Dr. Ivic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I told him that there were many cases of rape and that some of the women who had come to the clinic had agreed to be examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you want Dr. Ivic to do?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: So we talked about the possibility of Dr. Ivic taking them to the gynaecological ward in Prijedor so that the allegations could be established. And we hoped that this would put an end to the rapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he agree that these women could go to Prijedor, to the specialist ward?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: He wasn't able to give me an answer right away, but I think that it was on the following day that he came and told me that he would take the women to Prijedor. So a number of women, I don't know exactly how many, probably more than five but less than ten, were taken by him to Prijedor to be examined. When I talked to him on a subsequent occasion, the women had been brought back. I didn't see the findings, the results, of the examination. But he told me that all of these women had indeed been raped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, how difficult was it from your knowledge of the mentality and the upbringing for Bosniak women to complain of rape?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Personally, I think that it was a very small number of women who decided to come to the clinic and admit that they had been raped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Kuruzovic about the fact that, or attempt to see Kuruzovic, about the fact that apparently people were being allowed in to the camp to take women away?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I never spoke to Kuruzovic about this. Usually if we talked, there was also a man called Slavko Puhalic. I think he was Kuruzovic's deputy. He used to come to the clinic quite often, so we tried to use him to send messages to Kuruzovic for something to be done. But I can't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remember having any conversation about this with anyone apart from Dr. Dusko Ivic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as a result of your conversations with either the doctor or Mr. Puhalic, who you thought was the deputy, was anything done to stop these people coming in?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: After a while, these cases of women being raped abated in intensity. There was a number of tank operators, military personnel, the group referred to itself as "El Manijakos". That was the inscription they had on their tanks apparently. I think Kuruzovic then passed the message on and tried to keep these things from happening so often. One day, they arrived with two tanks. They quarrelled with Kuruzovic and Puhalic asking why they had allowed those women to be taken for examination. At any rate, following that, I was not really familiar with any more substantial number of rapes, but I do know that those same people then went around the surrounding villages looking for women to rape.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you become aware of a rape outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember there was a woman with a child who came to the camp. And she reported to the clinic. I was the person she talked to. She could barely walk. At the checkpoint in Orlovci, she was stopped by the guards. And then for ten consecutive days, she was raped by all of them. One night, she managed to escape with her child through a window. The next day, after she talked to me already, a lieutenant came. I think his name was Cumba. He was an active military officer. I think he was an MP, a military policeman, with another man, an inspector I think, who had a crest of white hair on top of his head. They asked questions about this particular woman, whether she had reported to us, the woman from Orlovci, because they wanted her apparently to testify to the effect that she had been raped. I decided not to tell them about her conversation with me, and I advised this woman to leave the camp on the next convoy and to go and see a physician once safe, once outside the Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The inspector that was there, did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: He wanted to have a word with me alone, so we went to the back room of the clinic. He warned me that all those working against Serbs would be killed. And he warned me to mind my actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, before I move to the next topic, can I ask you this: What sort of supplies were you given in the camp, medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I remembered the name, Skrbic, the soldier who came to the clinic in Kozarac. His name was Skrbic. I still can't remember his first name. His father's name was Skrbic, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I think you just proved that if you stop thinking about something, you'll remember it. All right. Medical supplies, please, at your clinic in Trnopolje. Were you provided with any?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We did not get any supplies before the arrival of the International Red Cross, only what we found upon our arrival there in the clinic in Trnopolje, that's what we used. Sometimes we would have an opportunity to join the guards in their rounds of the surrounding houses and find some medicines there to take back to the clinic in the camp. The only thing we ever got from Dr. Ivic was a flea powder, DDT.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any -- I'm sorry, let me rephrase it. Was there any violence in the camp being carried on against the inmates?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At some point soon, one of the rooms in the clinic that was supposed to be used as a lab but was not being used as a lab was used for interrogations and beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, who was being taken for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, camp inmates. I'm not sure based on what criteria. Perhaps they had lists. I'm not sure how they decided on who to take and who not. Mainly men, though. I never saw them take a single woman for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you know that the room that was supposed to be a lab was being used for beatings?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As I've just explained, this room is inside the clinic. It's part of the clinic, so it's perhaps 5 or 6 metres away between the two windows, the distance between the two windows. So you could hear the sounds of beatings going on, people being hit, people moaning. You could hear Serbs verbally abusing the people beaten because the distance was so small. Secondly, some of the people they beat would afterward be taken to the clinic for us to dress their wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you remember any particular - don't worry about names - but any particular injuries suffered by people?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Normally, blunt-force trauma. They kicked those people, they hit them with poles, wooden poles. There were injuries, wounds, cuts by knives apparently. Ejub Hrnic suffered a cut like that, I'm not sure if it was the left or the right leg. Near his knee, a bit lower, a nerve was severed. So he couldn't move his foot. He always dragged his foot behind him. He had other injuries, too. But this was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you or someone else actually have a camera with you at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Azra Blazevic had a camera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you able to photograph any of the injuries that you saw?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We talked once when beatings became very frequent. We talked about an opportunity to photograph the injuries of those people so that someday we could prove what had happened. And we were very much in two minds whether we should try to do that or not because we were in danger of being caught doing it. We agreed that only very few of us, the people who were working in the clinic, would know about it. And then we decided -- we decided not to take photographs so that the people who had been beaten would not say that someone was then taking their photographs. So, for example, I suppose most people know about this now, but it may be the case that someone who was there in the clinic could say: "No, they didn't take any photographs at all," because they didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, just so we understand. I think I understand what you're saying. In other words, if they were interrogated by guards, they wouldn't be able to say that their injuries were being photographed.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Precisely. We wanted to reduce the risk to the minimum and wanted to have as few people know about this as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you said that it was happening once the beatings became very frequent. Can you tell us when that -- what period that was roughly?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That was in June, July, until the arrival of journalists. That was the toughest period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were those -- did those beatings happen only during interrogation, or were there beatings that took place outside of interrogations?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what they did over there, were those official interrogations or were they just beating people. Most of the people I know had been beaten would first be accused of owning a weapon or being a member of the Green Berets or having hidden their money. But I'm not sure why they picked particular people to be beaten as opposed to other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did any beatings take place outside the -- that room in the clinic? In other words, in the open?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, also outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was doing the beating? Was it the guards or people who came into the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, they went into a boiler room in the school building, and they beat the people they found there. I don't think those were the guards who were on guard duty at that point, but other people who arrived there. On another occasion, we watched from our window when they brought people from Keraterm, and then Zigic arrived. He had the Keraterm people lined up. He said: "God help you heroes." And they answered: "God help you, too." He called out -- he called one of the men to step forward and told him: "Come out, come forward." And then he made him go down on his knees, and he kicked him and beat him until the man fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Zigic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him, and he did not come to Trnopolje, at least not that I knew. That was the only time he came, with the Keraterm camp inmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who told you what his name was?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Someone from the clinic knew him. I was not born in Prijedor myself, so I didn't know people's names there. But Azra and those other people who were born in Prijedor knew them. And he was a taxi driver, so people knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the guards make any attempt to stop Zigic or any of the other people who were --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, no. No one even tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think, and this may be the appropriate moment to start looking at them, although I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know what time Your Honour is intending to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have ten minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can start on the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were able, as we will see, to provide to Penny Marshall I think a film that had been taken during the time at Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Her first arrival I think it was in early August, possibly the 4th of August, we managed to hand over the film.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I want you to look, please, at some of the photographs that came off this film. But first of all, one that's a slightly separate one. And that's the photograph --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour was given a huge -- another bundle. I hope this one as well. There was one that was shown to the witness. I think it's a new one. 01035318. Your Honour, it's separate. It's not taken -- it's not from the roll of film. It's a separate number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just identify that. I think you were shown it by the investigator.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This, to the left, is a shop that was outside the clinic, but it's all in one building. And the part to the right is the clinic, the door, and the phone lines. And what you can see behind in the back is the large hall. And this photo was taken from the north side, from the school building. And this was probably after the camp had been closed down because the UN never came to the camp during the camp's operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we see where the lab was, in this photograph, that was used for the beatings?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, not from this side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not from this side, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless there's an objection, may that be marked Exhibit S321-3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we start looking at some of the photographs that you provided or that were on the film. Could we have a look at the one that was marked 01035329, which looks like that.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The upper half, you can see Mujo, a sanitary technician, a paramedic who was with us, standing next to him is a patient who I think spent a night or two at the clinic. Here you can see Hase Dzolagic. He's a vet. This here, that's myself. And these were taken at the Kozarac clinic. The way you can see Mujo lying here, that's how we slept in our clothes on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These were taken at the Kozarac clinic, what, during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: My apologies. This is Trnopolje, not Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be then admitted as Exhibit S321-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any objections. Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, could you have a look, please, at 01035330.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In the lower picture, you can see Azra Blazevic, the vet. And the other picture, you can see Sefik Karabasic. And you can see how we had to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were any beds ever provided for you in the clinic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, no beds whatsoever. We had two beds for examinations of our patients, but those had been there from before. And Babica the midwife slept on one of them, and the other one was usually used by Mujo to sleep on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that then be marked 321-5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No objections. Therefore, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, then at 01035331.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -6. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In the upper photo, you can see Babica, the midwife, and in the lower photograph you can see Vasif Gutic. And in the background, you can see Goga, the Serb woman who stayed with us all the time, even during the early stage of our stay in Trnopolje. At some point, they told her she had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's 6. And then the next one, please: 01035337.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This is Nedzad Jakupovic. We managed to take a photograph of him once. He was brought back from that room which was used for the beatings. I think they only brought him to the clinic because of the wound to his eye. So we had an opportunity to take a photograph, and we did. As you can see, this is not a frontal view because we didn't want the patient to notice that he was being photographed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections? -7.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. -7. There were no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to ask a couple of questions about that, this man. The laceration to the eye, we can see that you dressed. And the injuries to his body. Do you remember whether there were any other injuries which we can't see in the photograph? To his wrists, for example.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to diagnose. There was a fracture. Yes. That's right. He had wire marks cut into the skin of his arms. And then he told us that his arms had been tied with wire during the beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether there was anyone else, any other prisoner with him in the interrogation room?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were two other inmates with him, I think. One was killed as a result of the beating. And I don't know anything about the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. And I'm sorry, the other photograph, which I should have put in first, is 01035336.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is also a photo of Nedzad Jakupovic, only taken from a different angle. Perhaps it's a pity that we didn't get a frontal view. His face was bleeding and bruised. But we just couldn't take a photograph of the front side of his body.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to have the break now. The trial stays adjourned until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.59 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And first of all, our apologies for being late. But unexpected, we had to contact a visitor, a diplomat, from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as it was for the purpose of this case, we gave priority to this. Once again, our apologies. And please, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If we can just complete the series of photographs, please, Doctor. Could you now be shown the one numbered 01035338.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -9, yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what that shows us, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The microphone is not on at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: On this picture, we see the Trnopolje camp. The photograph was taken from the direction of the clinic yard facing south, that is. And the shop which used to sell construction material which was operative before the war over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough idea of when that was taken, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This picture was taken before the visit of the journalists, so it must have been sometime in June or July, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then -- thank you. If you can be given the next photograph in sequence, 339, which is the same area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was taken from the same direction, that is, from the building where the clinic was, facing the community centre, facing south. And again, the construction material shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Doctor. There are two more effectively of that -- well, there's one more of that, which I don't think I'm going to trouble to put in. But could you be shown 01035341, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -11. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's taken, I think, from a slightly different angle.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes indeed. This was taken, compared to the other photographs, more to the right. On the left side, we see a portion of the house which used to be a construction material shop. So this is more to the right with respect to this house, compared to the previous photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we just ask you this: It's quite difficult to tell. Can we see some sort of wire there, or is that just a trick of the printing or the negative?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There is a wire from the construction material shop, the wire that used to be there in place before. But one cannot see it on this photograph, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry. There's a line going across what looks like the top of the pole, but that's --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not the wire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. And then could you look, please, at 01035342.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This depicts one of the truck convoys which was organised in Trnopolje. Since these are the trucks, I think this was taken some time in late July because the first convoys were organised in cattle cars. And it was only later that they were organised with trucks. This was taken from the clinic yard, from the area outside the clinic facing east, and the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then -- have we got a number? Then 01035343.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This again is one of the convoys. Probably the last truck of the convoy, and you can see the detainees boarding the truck. This was taken from the same angle. This is the yard, the area outside the clinic. I think you can see a soldier here standing guard with a rifle. And then a second one who had a uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to correct myself. This is -13.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. 01035344.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a man from the village of Hrnici, I believe, the area of Trnopolje. He was also in the room where the beatings usually took place. He lost considerable weight. He was once taken to the clinic for us to examine him, and that is when we managed to take this photograph. He died later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Died where, in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When he died, were you asked to examine the body?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, not when he died. He was taken in a horse-drawn cart, I believe. He was taken away. And one of the detainees had to bury him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was he one of the prisoners who had come from either Omarska or Keraterm, or was he in Trnopolje throughout?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: He had been in Trnopolje throughout that period of time. He was not one of -- from this group from either Keraterm or Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And finally, of this group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not to forget, this would be -14. But in order to come back to this question, if I may, did you see this person earlier in a better state of health, and what is your diagnosis the fact that this person has lost the weight? Was it caused by the fact that this person was in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sure that this was the result of his stay in Trnopolje. He suffered from dysentery. He must have been tortured, and he probably lost a lot of weight as a result of that. And that was the cause of his death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the final, 01035345. Is that the same man?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same man. Here you can see the lower part of his body. As you can see, here again, we took photograph from the backside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's 15, I think, Your Honour. 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, it's -15 already. And may I ask, because I didn't in the past, any objections against the admission into evidence of the pictures shown until now which is 321-15?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can I ask you to look at two other photographs, please, which are contained in the bundle Exhibit S15. The first is S15-14.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I believe that this photograph was also taken in Trnopolje, although not by us. It depicts one of the detainees who had arrived either from Keraterm or Omarska. At any rate, he was not detained in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we look, then, at the next photograph, S15-15.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This was also taken in Trnopolje, but not by us. It was after the visit of the journalists. It depicts one of the men who had arrived from either Omarska or Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then could I ask you to look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I gather, Your Honour, this one hasn't yet been given an Exhibit Number. Is bears the number 00452507 in the same bundle. It should be very close. If the bundle is organised the same as ours, it follows 2537.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, because I don't have this photograph before me, it's in the bundle S15?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we have the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S15-41. Objections? I can't see any. Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that scene, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I cannot find my bearings here on this photograph. I really cannot tell you what it is exactly. It must have been taken in Trnopolje camp, but I cannot tell you for sure. I don't have any reference point in the background. But I assume that it was taken in Trnopolje after the arrival of the men from Omarska and Keraterm. But again, I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, technically the witness not having recognised, I'm not sure we can call evidence, perhaps we can deal with it by admission from the Defence that it is one of the series that was taken from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Observations by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly we cannot confirm nor deny. But if the witness didn't recognise it, then we think that it shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you withdraw. I think there is no additional probative value.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, on diagrams and photographs, Doctor, I think you also produced a diagram of some of the buildings in Trnopolje for the investigator with the number 01035316.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: On this diagram, we can see the clinic together with the adjacent building in Trnopolje. In front of the building here, on the right-hand Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. side, there was a shop on the ground floor which had a separate entrance. There was also a small shed, a small warehouse belonging to the shop. This was the entrance to the clinic. There was a corridor here on the right-hand side. And on the left side where I'm showing, was the room where the laboratory used to be. This is where they used to beat people. These are the three rooms which were used as examination rooms in the clinic. This was also a small shed. And here are the premises of the local commune which consisted of two rooms, one on the left side and one on the right-hand side. Here, there was a cafe on the ground floor. And on the upper floor, there were the premises of the football club. There was an entrance to the cafe, and there was a stairway leading up to the football club. There was a community hall belonging to the community centre behind. The entrance was on the left-hand side over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The area here is the yard outside the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which was the room in which the beatings took place?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This one, this one here. It was to the left with respect to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I forgot when I was dealing with the photographs that you took, or rather -- because I didn't have it there to ask you to look at 01035334.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Once again, to interrupt you, but maybe it was my misunderstanding. I understood that the three rooms to the right-hand side where you can read "exam" on the first room, the rooms marked 1, 2, and 3, that they were used for examination and beatings. Now I understood it would be the room marked with capital A. Could you please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's wrong. The room A, marked with A, that was the room used for the beatings. And rooms 1, 2, and 3 were rooms in which we examined the patients and in which we stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you look, please, at the next photograph, I think which I've already asked, which is 334.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, not too fast. May we first give this sketch --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- The number 322. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S322.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, could you have a look, please, at this photograph and tell us first of all what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This is just the room, the room marked as Room A. We managed once to photograph this room immediately after one of the beatings. This is the inside of that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that be marked -- whatever the number was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 16. S321, in the line of the photographs, S321-16, with the ERN number ending with 334.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive us, we got up to 9 on that series of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Under S321, we continued until 15. 14 and 15 depicted --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour is right. We're wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then 16. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown the number 5335.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the same room from a different angle. You can see bloodstains on the wall and on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, thank you. I think that is all the photographs now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, did people die as a result of the beatings? You've already talked about that man who died, although you said it was more through dysentery. What about anybody else?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Teofik Talic, another man who was killed in that room. He died as a result of the beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any other deaths that happened in Trnopolje caused not as a result of natural causes, but by some kind of outside agency?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were other cases, too. There was a man suffering from epileptic fits. We didn't have the proper medicines to treat him. He had a fit once, and the only thing we had were tranquilisers. I asked Ivic to have the right medicine brought there or to take the man to the Prijedor hospital. Ivic failed to do that, and as a result the man died the next morning. There was another case where a woman was killed by a firearm outside the school building. There were a number of cases in which camp inmates would be taken outside the camp, as opposed to inside the camp, and killed there. Those were the most frequent cases, inmates being killed outside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you recall the names of any particular people who were killed in that way, i.e., taken outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: One day, they had the inmates lined up outside the school building. They had lists. They looked at those lists. They were looking for the last name Foric. I think they singled out about five or six people with that last name and took them towards Ribnjak. I heard later they were killed there on the same day. Murgic, father and son, their last name was Murgic, they were killed. They were Croats. They were tortured. And also, somewhere towards Ribnjak and Mlin, across the railroad track they were killed there. Murgic's wife was a Serb. She had come to the camp looking for her husband and child. She came to the clinic and spoke to us, but we were not allowed to tell her that they had been killed. We didn't dare. We were afraid that she would later go to someone else and tell them that she had found out from us about their death. And then questions would be asked about how we had learned. Pero Curguz, the head of the Serbian Red Cross, would select inmates from the camp to perform burials of dead bodies. We heard about a number of such cases. The first next village on the way to Prijedor, Elezi, bodies were being collected there. 20 persons were killed there, both men and women, and they were buried near the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a topic that you touched on earlier, and that's the question of convoys, and we looked at a couple of photographs. You said that as the camp got fuller, convoys of people would be taken out. How often would these convoys go during the period that you were in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. They cleansed village by village. In the following manner, a unit would enter a village, round up the men, separate them from the women and children, and then women and children would be taken to Trnopolje, as a rule, as far as I know. And as for the men, they had special lists on the basis of which they decided to send them to Omarska or to Keraterm. And then later, they would perhaps be taken to Trnopolje. And once the camp there was filled to capacity, there would be convoys for women and children to be transferred in order to make room inside the camp for those cleansed from the next village. And this procedure would be repeated over and over again. And every time the camp was filled up with Muslim men. So gradually the number of Muslim men inside the camp increased because men were not allowed to leave the camp. An exception could be made here and there if among the women, there was anyone who had good Serb friends, they could try to contact them and try to persuade them to allow their men to join one of the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say "men weren't allowed to leave the camp." Were they kept in closer confinement than the women and children?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't think you could call it "closer confinement." They were all in the same compound except that the school building was always reserved for men. But that could change if there was a need to allow women into the school building to let them stay there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that they cleansed village by village and described how that happened. Is that what you learned from the people who came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, we learned this from those people who had been picked up. They would come and they would always tell us the same story.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From that, the fact that you were being told the same story over and over again, what conclusion did you come as to what was happening here?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm certain that this was planned at the top level and that orders came from up high. I don't think that an ordinary military officer could cleanse the whole area in a matter of two or three months and kill as many people as they did. As I said, once they entered the village, they have lists of persons to be killed. I have no idea why they did, but they always had lists with precise instructions as to how to deal with a certain individual. So this also confirms that the whole thing must have been carefully planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did there seem to be any difference in the treatment of villages where there had been some kind of resistance from the non-Serbs and those where there had not, in the description of what had happened?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There was no difference whatsoever. As I've told you, when they collected bodies from Elezi, near Trnopolje, it was no earlier than July. And Serbs were there, too. And the same thing happened to them as happened perhaps in other places to people who tried to put up some sort of resistance. No matter whether there was any armed resistance or not, it always ended the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that a lot of the time you spoke to the gentleman who appeared to be Kuruzovic's deputy. But did you from time to time speak to Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, yes, I did. But I can't remember any details now. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about the details, but when you were speaking to him, did you ever have any reference made by him to, as it were, other authorities?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Concerning the organising of convoys and certain decisions, but most often we would hear this sort of thing from Slavko Puhalic, the fact that they had to wait for approval first and for decisions at a higher level so that those decisions could then be implemented. So we heard from Slavko Puhalic, I think, that there was supposed to be a session of some body, the session was supposed to decide whether 3 per cent of the Muslim population would be allowed to stay, to remain in the Prijedor area. This clearly indicates that decisions were being made elsewhere, and it didn't really appear to me that Major Kuruzovic was the one making decisions concerning the fate of those people there. Even the arrival of journalists only took place as far as I know after Karadzic had granted his approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about one particular convoy about which you later heard that the people had been killed. Did you see the loading of the people that eventually you heard were killed on Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That was, I think, the last convoy to leave Trnopolje. And that was when the International Red Cross had already announced their arrival. I think, in fact, that the representatives of the International Red Cross had already arrived in Trnopolje, but the camp inmates had not been registered yet. So over the next two days, this convoy was organised which could be joined freely by men, whoever could fit on to the lorries and buses. Up to that point, it was only on rare occasions that any of the men managed to smuggle themselves out. But this time, they could join.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when the men were being put on to that convoy, did you see them being put there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. They would always put people on convoys either on the Prijedor/Trnopolje/Kozarac Road or further down the road, the Trnopolje/Prijedor -- the lower road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've looked earlier at the two photographs, one of the lorries, as it were, and one of the people being loaded on. Are you able to say whether that photograph was a photograph of the, if I can call it that, the Mount Vlasic convoy, or another? Or if you're not sure, say so.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think that's another convoy, a different one. That's not the convoy for Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember whether or not Major Kuruzovic was there when this man -- I'm sorry, when the men were being put on to the trucks?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Major Kuruzovic was there with brothers Balaban. They were twins. And I think, as far as I know, they were his bodyguards. The fact that younger people, younger men, were taken off the convoy and killed on Mount Vlasic, we learned this through the radio. When Penny Marshall came, the second time she came, she gave us as a present a radio set which was tuned in to the frequency of the Sarajevo radio. And we heard that on the radio. The interesting thing is that the following day, they wanted to organise another convoy. But people refused to join it once they had heard the news that those people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, just to jump ahead for a moment, and then I'm going to deal with Penny Marshall's visit. I think you left Trnopolje on the 30th of September, one of the last people to leave. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct, the last day of September. We turned up in Karlovac the following day. I think it was the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you got on to the bus to take you out of Trnopolje, did you see anybody from that convoy, the one that had gone over Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was only in the bus that I learned that the International Red Cross in some way, I don't know how, had managed to get five people out of Banja Luka, evacuate them, people who had survived the Vlasic massacre. They spirited them into Trnopolje and loaded them on to one of the buses. I talked to those people. And what they told me roughly was that they were being -- that soldiers were entering the buses and lorries requiring that the younger men inside the buses should get off so that more space would be left inside for the women and children. And when the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, forgive me, I'm going to stop you. The Court has heard evidence from the people who survived or from some of them. So we needn't to go through what you were told. But all I wanted to check was you saw those people when you got on to the bus?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were on the last bus with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just before we deal with the visit by Penny Marshall and the other journalists, can I ask you this: In summary form, the day that the journalists or the day before the journalists arrived, what were the conditions in the camp like?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You mean the day before, or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, and then I'll ask you what they did the day -- I'm sorry, it's my fault again. Generally speaking, what were the conditions in the camp like? How would you sum them up in the period immediately before the journalists came?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I've tried to divide the period inside the camp into three different periods of time. The most difficult period for us was before the arrival of the journalists. And then the period between the visit of the journalists and then the arrival of the International Red Cross. And then the third period between the arrival of the International Red Cross and the closing of the camp. The first period, I think, was the most difficult one because anyone would be allowed into the camp, take away any of the prisoners inside the camp, beat them. There was no safety. There was no food. So generally speaking, that period was the most difficult one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you -- before the journalists arrived, were any preparations made by the camp authorities?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Azra also learned from one of the guards that journalists would perhaps arrive for a visit, which means that the guards knew already. So preparations were carried out. A wire fence was put up between the construction material shop and the dom building where the inmates from Keraterm were later accommodated. And then the one outside the shop is where they later put inmates from Omarska. We were put in a special place -- they were put in a special place, and Major Kuruzovic told us that those were really dangerous people and that we should keep away from them. Whenever one of those persons tried to go to the clinic, they would always have the person marched over to the clinic by one of the guards. That was before they took the wire fence down. Later, when various delegations began to arrive and visit the camp and further journalists, they took the wire fencing down. And they allowed people to move about in the camp and across the way from the camp. You could -- people were allowed to put up small tents there, those who had no room inside the school building or inside the dom building. So the situation improved in that period, after the visit of the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But before the visit of the journalists, you say Azra learned about them, were any special preparations made by the camp authorities? What, for example, happened to the women and children?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: A convoy was organised for them. So when the journalists arrived, there were extremely few women and children left. The women who had been brought in from Omarska before the journalists arrived, those were also taken to Prijedor at that point. So when the journalists arrived, the women who had been brought into this camp from Omarska were no longer there. That was the convoy of women that left at that point, and they allowed some of the sick and wounded to join that convoy, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going to have a look at a brief excerpt from the film that was shot by ITN on that visit. Then, on the return visit by Penny Marshall after it had been shown on television. And I think subsequently, you also gave, I think, an interview to an American news programme, ABC Nightline. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Translation?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, what we've done, and I'm going to ask the film be played now, we've extracted from the various things the excerpts which are relevant. At some point, we've had to -- you'll see particularly with the American programme, we have to take out other people who were speaking. It has been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The video as such would then be S --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. The video as such would be then S323. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there's a transcript that we have had done. Some of it is not very easy to follow. One in English and one in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -1A and -1B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, I know you've had a look at it before, but if there's any comment that you want to make, perhaps you just lean into the microphone and say stop, and then the technicians will stop playing it and you can make your comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Otherwise, I would ask that the video now be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. May I ask whether the public gallery also a screen is available that we have public access? Because we have a visitor in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Your Honour, I don't know. I think it's only about a two-chair public gallery from what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. Do you agree that we proceed? Thank you. The visitor in the public gallery waived his right to see this video. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause for one moment. I'm sorry, can we just roll it back because I want to ask a question. I'm sorry, can you just play -- I want to ask about one of the people in the video. Pause, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, Doctor, I should have asked, what are we looking at here?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Here we see the patients standing around the person wearing the white coat. This is Mico Kobas, a Serb, the man who is missing one arm. Here, he had arrived with the journalists. Mico Kobas was a paramedic. This picture was taken in the waiting hall at the Trnopolje clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, what was the problem here, if there was a problem?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The problem here was the fact that Mico Kobas was with them as part of the escort. So we were not allowed to say anything. We didn't want him to hear certain things. I was trying to hide behind the cameraman so that Mico would not see me. I motioned to Penny Marshall to indicate that she should try and move him away so that we can continue the conversation without his presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the second visit of Penny Marshall. Here you can see clearly that the fence had been completely taken off. That's all what I wanted to say. She is coming, as we can see, from the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. If we can continue playing the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause for a moment, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, Doctor, who is the man we can see behind you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's Vasif Gutic, who at the time was a student at the school of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And on this second visit when Penny Marshall came back and showed you the English newspapers, was there anybody present from the Serbs, or were you on your own?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, there were no Serbs present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Your Honour, then the next clip that we're going to see comes from the American programme, the ABC news. Yes, if we could carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It helped us a lot since immediately after that, the situation improved. They brought down the wire. They started bringing a little food."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Please stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said at one point in time that Muslims could use the train. I was referring to the visits because there were still people in Prijedor who had not been rounded up or detained who had families in Trnopolje. They were not allowed to come to Trnopolje to board the train there, to visit their family there before that. But later on, they were allowed to do that. I was referring to the visitors, not to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes. The video can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the woman who is talking now?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The woman talking is Azra Blazevic, the veterinarian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, if we can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Narrator: You can see that threat mirrored on the face of Dr. Idriz, who ran the Trnopolje clinic. "Journalist: Have you had any cases here of people who had bean beaten in the other camp? "The Witness: [Interpretation] They just saw me shrug. I just shrugged and said nothing. Of course, one was not allowed to speak. You always had a guide. "Narrator: Today, Dr. Idriz is safe in the refugee camp at Karlovac. Today, he can tell the truth about Trnopolje. "The Witness: [Interpretation] In the camp, some people died from beatings. Others died because we weren't allowed to take them to hospital. There were a lot of people taken out of the camp and killed. "Narrator: In all, Dr. Idriz says, about 200 men were killed at Trnopolje, and beatings, he says, were constant. Nedzad's battered body was photographed this summer by Dr. Idriz. "The Witness: [Interpretation] We didn't actually see the beatings. But we were in the room next to where they were taking place. We could hear the beating, and the crying. "Narrator: Dr. Idriz says the Trnopolje camp military commander once tried to discipline a rapist. "The Witness: [Interpretation] When the rest of the soldiers found out about that, they got drunk and drove two tanks in front of the main military barracks and gave an ultimatum that the soldier had to be released or else they would shoot at their own barracks. So they released the soldier. "As soon as the people came, they were just pushed into the camp. They were left to organise themselves."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's the end of the excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, just one question on what we heard you say. The incident you described on tape about the tanks being driven in front of the office of the commander and demanding the release of the barracks, was that the same incident you were -- demanding the release of one of their comrades, was that the incident you earlier described to us with the tank regiment?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the event in question. They had arrived in Trnopolje in order to discuss why the women had been taken out to undergo an examination at all. Later we heard stories, I don't know whether they were correct or not, that one of their soldiers was detained because of that in the Prijedor barracks. And that the rest of the group went to the barracks in two tanks and released this colleague of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally can we deal with very briefly with matters after the visits of the journalists. The International Red Cross, I think, came in around the 15th of August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in mid-August, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After that, did they register the people in the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Not on the first day. A couple of days later, people who happened to be in the camp were registered. Each of them received a registration booklet, an ID of sorts, with a registration number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did the food and medical supplies improve after they arrived?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The International Red Cross organised a complete delivery of food on a daily basis, and we also received all the medicine that we needed. The supplies came directly to me, I mean, they would first come to see me, and then I would tell them what kind of medicine we needed, and that would subsequently be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And eventually, was the camp closed down as far as you were aware on the 30th of September when you left?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The camp was officially closed down, although there remained a few people, including women and children, who were not registered, people who had arrived in the camp later on with the hope of being registered which would in turn enable them to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before being allowed on to the bus, were you made to sign any kind of papers?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No one could leave the camp without previously signing a certificate to the effect that they were thereby abandoning all their property to Serbs. We all received a copy of this paper. I had one, too, but unfortunately I tore it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to the property that you owned in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: My property and the property of the majority of Muslims was destroyed. According to what I know about what happened usually, after the cleansing, Serbs would take with them whatever they needed, whatever they wanted to take. It did depend on the village and the town. But, for example, I started to build a house in the old town of Prijedor, the old neighbourhood of Prijedor, where most of the Muslims lived. This area was completely razed to the ground. You cannot even find any foundations there. All mosques and Croatian churches were blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During your time at Trnopolje, were you ever beaten yourself?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness also stated that what happened in the old town of Prijedor had nothing to do with the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say: "What happened in the town of Prijedor had nothing to do with the war." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I mean that the destruction, the arson, the burning down of the houses, mosques, and Croatian churches occurred after the cleansing. The damage which is the result of the shelling is a completely different thing. You can argue that it was not intentional. But this, on the other hand, was done intentionally and according to a plan. My opinion is that the idea behind this kind of destruction was to prevent people from coming back because whoever had a house left standing would perhaps wish to come back. But if everything is destroyed, that certainly prevents people from coming back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you ever been back since 1992, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Doctor, you'll have to speak up again. Your reply was --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't. Since 1992, I haven't been back to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you receive any kind of death threats before you left Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Just before the camp was closed down, a day or two before the very end of the camp, I was approached by Mladen Mitrovic who told me that he had been given an order to kill me and that I should not be allowed to leave the camp alive. Later in the conversation, he told me that he was not going to do it, that he wouldn't do it. I don't know whether he was serious or whether he was only trying to scare me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you who had given him the order?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me whose order it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm very grateful to you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I come to the ongoing -- the question how to proceed, may I respectfully ask the representative of the OTP whether or not it was on purpose or whether I missed this issue in the statement of the witness given in the August 2000 on page 14, paragraph 2 as regards a Muslim family named Foric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He gave the evidence, Your Honour. He said they were taken out, the Forics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But we did not include, and therefore I want to come back to this, the sketch with the ER number 01035315.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. That was deliberate. But if Your Honour wants, certainly we can come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be helpful for a better understanding if we could just come back to this question and go into some details and base the explanation for a better understanding on this sketch which would be S3 -- Exhibit Number S324.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I just want to make sure I get the right diagram.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to explain how they took Forics out? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, please. If you would be so kind, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This is the clinic. The corridor is on this side of the building. There were windows on the corridor. This is the school building and the main entrance to the school. The detainees from the school building were lined up outside the school in several rows. Then names were called out. They said that those bearing the family name of Foric should come up. Five or six people came out, and the others were let go. The Forics were then taken along this road southward, towards the railway station. If my memory serves me right, they were taken in the direction of the mill which was located on this side of the road. And this is where they were killed. As for the Murgic people, they were taken to the pond which cannot be seen here. But you reach it via this road here. You have to pass by the railway station, and then you find yourself at a very large fish pond. So when they left the clinic, the area outside the clinic, they passed along this road moving towards the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does Your Honour want to any further -- may that then be produced as.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was S324. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these additional comments.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these additional comments based on this sketch. This facilitates our understanding of your testimony. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It's not possible to start with the cross-examination today. And therefore, we have to ask you, Doctor, to return tomorrow, 9.30, for the questions by the Defence. But I can see you have a question. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the name of Dragan Skrbic, father's name Ostoja. Dragan Skrbic was the soldier who came to the clinic in Kozarac. And Ostoja Skrbic was his father who was with Rade Baltic at one point in time. And there's one more addition that I wish to make regarding checkpoints and guard posts, when we discussed snipers and machine-gun nests. I should like to add that the guards were not always the same. They were rotated. Usually every two weeks, they would be rotated. They had with them their personal weapons, and depending on the shift and depending on the weapons there, the situation changed. I'm sure that there must have been guards who did not have machine-guns, for instance. So there must have been periods of time when the only weapons that they had were just personal, light weapons. So it really depended on the kind of the unit that was providing the security, that was doing the guard duty. That would be all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these additional remarks. And as mentioned beforehand, we are glad to know that you are prepared to hear and answer the questions by the Defence tomorrow from 9.30 in this same courtroom. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. And thank you very much for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the meantime, it remains for me to admit into evidence what has not yet been done. S15-37, -38, -39, -40, and S321-16 and -17. As regards now tomorrow, what is the expectation of the Defence? What's the estimated length of time for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll be able to finish our cross probably during the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll say during the first 90 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask, will Mr. Ostojic be present tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I spoke with him two hours ago, and he informed me that he wasn't able to book his flight back to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this causes a problem. It's envisaged that we, as planned and scheduled already last week, we have to finalise the testimony of Mr. Sebire. It's correct that he wants to leave, and he has to leave The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There was a slight misunderstanding by Mr. Koumjian. He was due to go away to interview witnesses last Sunday. Because of what happened, it was changed. So he is here at any stage from now on. So it's not vital from that point of view to hear him, but he's available and ready to testify tomorrow, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But as you all know, we have only one day available, and we have to use this day for the purposes of his testimony. We will receive additional material. And therefore, I think there is no other way than to proceed. We have already several times given some assistance to the Defence taking care when Mr. Ostojic was not able to be present. But I think the remaining questions can also be put to Mr. Sebire by you, Mr. Stakic [sic]. And I think, in fact, we should concentrate on that what will have the highest probative value. And this is the new table, hopefully to be concluded by tomorrow based on the persons named in the attachment of the fourth amended indictment. Can we agree that we proceed after we have concluded the testimony of Mr. Merdzanic, that we then continue with the testimony of Mr. Sebire?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's no problem from our side, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would rather not, Your Honour. But if you rule that way, we'll comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary for the reasons given before. And if there should be remaining questions, no doubt, a solution will be found that allows the Defence to put these additional questions, if any, to the witness. So therefore, I would ask the OTP to be prepared tomorrow that Mr. Sebire appears hopefully. And I heard, and rumours were -- on the basis of rumours, that he did work during the entire weekend in preparation of the new table. Hopefully he can provide us with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he worked all night as well as the weekend, Your Honour, so I think he can. May I just mention one other thing, really Mr. Koumjian's appearance reminded me of this, Your Honour made an order of the translation of Mr. Corin's report. It should be done within seven days. Does that include the French? Because I think there will be a problem on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, it's the right of the Defence and Dr. Stakic himself. So therefore, absolute priority is given to B/C/S, and then as fast as possible, please, the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Just so that we know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Anything in addition prepared for tomorrow? Because it may be that we have additional time available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. As Your Honour knows I have been appearing and disappearing saying: "Can I have a legal argument or a legal discussion." I know Your Honour said of course it should be for all three Judges to hear, I wonder if we could adopt the procedure rather like yesterday's where we use up the time where I can address Your Honours. And Your Honours, without making any sort of ruling until Judge Fassi Fihri is back, will get the general gist of the submissions I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try and see whether or not this can be possible. We come back to this tomorrow. And I hope that no other issues in this case or in the other case will have priority and demand your presence maybe --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understand what has happened today, there will be no decisions being made tomorrow. And Mr. Cayley will be able to deal with whatever happens first thing tomorrow morning. So as I say, I'm grateful to Your Honour for the extra ten minutes, but I should be covered for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then finally for today, because it has to be prepared - we discussed it already briefly - it is envisaged that, always worst-case thinking, in case Judge Fassi Fihri - we all don't hope - will not be available by next Monday. But we know that the witness summoned for Monday and Tuesday has a very tight time frame and schedule. And therefore, would it be agreeable for the parties that we, for this purpose, act under Rule 71. This would say that we would take a deposition. We would assign one of the Judges in this case as responsible for taking this interview but, at the same time, granting all the procedural rights for the parties, the same method of interviewing this person, and at the same time the possibility for cross-examination for Defence. And then later on, Judge Fassi Fihri is available again, introduce the result of this deposition into the hearing. Would this be an agreeable method of working for the parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I prefer to hear what the Defence have to say first. And then I will respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are okay with that kind of procedure, so we don't have any objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, again, it's the same. If the Defence waive any objections, then we are not going to raise an objection either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we try to proceed this way, still hoping that we can continue with the three of us on Monday. Please understand that I can't inform you right now whether or not we have a hearing on Thursday and Friday. It would be premature. Unfortunately, I didn't have any contact with Judge Fassi Fihri during the lunch break. I will inform you as soon as possible what will happen on Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would have severe problems over witnesses. Mr. Brown, who - Your Honour having said that he will now be giving evidence next week - requires quite a lot of preparation to sort out the documents. And he won't be ready to give evidence on Thursday. That's the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Let's consider this question. First, have all facts together and then decide. This is the normal way it goes. So may I ask, any mandatory issues for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour. It would be fair to Mr. Ostojic to tell him not to come if there is nothing on Thursday and Friday because he would come here for no working days. So I would ask Your Honours to provide us really as soon as possible the information so we can inform my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I will try to do this within the next two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks a lot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Anything from your side?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This concludes today's hearing, this 70th day of this hearing. And the trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.30.
